newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Tambrands CEO sees focus abroad.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Tambrands CEO sees focus abroad.

text.p: Tambrands Inc chief executive and president Edward Fogarty said on Wednesday the company's restructuring plan was part of a larger effort to expand abroad.
Fogarty, who was named chairman Wednesday morning, told Reuters the company's best opportunity for growth was in emerging markets.
"We are taking a truly global view of the business," he said. "The really big opportunity over the longer haul is the developing part of the world and emerging markets."

Earlier Wednesday, the maker of tampons and feminine hygiene products said it would take a pre-tax charge of $46 million, or $1.00 per share in the third quarter, and that it would close four plants and cut its workforce by about 17 percent.
The restructuring will result in pre-tax annual savings of about $20 million, to be recognized in 1998. Fogarty said he calculated the savings to be about $0.30 per share.
He said the company may put some of the savings into new product launches.

"If we have a very attractive new product that would require incremental marketing support to launch, we would seriously consider taking part of that annual savings," he said. But he said that scenario was purely "hypothetical" at this point.
Fogarty also said Tambrands has no immediate plans to diversify its product.

"Not for the time being because we continue to believe there is a heck of an opportunity in the tampon business," he said. "My feeling is short-term diversification would just distract all of us from the job at hand which is to grow the tampon market."
As part of the restructuring, Thomas Mason, who was named chief operating officer, would oversee the company's Americas and international groups which will be combined into a single operation.
Fogarty said the initial global efforts would focus on Russia, Brazil and Italy.
The recent pricing pressure in the U.S. market had no effect on the decision to cut costs, he said.
"The pricing situation is really improving and it has nothing to do with the restructuring announcement," Fogarty said. "The restructuring was purely a function of having too much capacity."
The company's stock rose 1-1/8 to close at 42-7/8.
